question: Under Minnesota law, who is required to wear a DOT-approved helmet while riding a motorcycle?
choice_a: Operators and passengers under age 18, and anyone riding on a motorcycle instruction permit
choice_c: No one -- helmet use is entirely optional for all riders
explanation: Minnesota law requires operators and passengers under 18 years of age, and anyone operating on a motorcycle permit, to wear a DOT-approved helmet. The Department of Public Safety strongly recommends helmet use for all riders and passengers.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.V, 'Motorcycle Operating Rules' and 'Helmets'

question: According to the manual, about how many motorcycle crashes result in head or neck injuries?
explanation: One out of every five motorcycle crashes results in head or neck injuries, and these injuries account for a majority of serious and fatal injuries to motorcyclists.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.2, 'Wear the Right Gear'

question: A DOT-compliant helmet lets a rider see how far to the sides?
choice_a: Less than half of a rider's natural field of view
choice_b: Only straight ahead, with no peripheral vision at all
choice_c: As far as necessary -- studies show a helmet does not keep a rider from spotting danger
choice_d: Only to one side, depending on helmet style
explanation: A DOT-compliant helmet lets you see as far to the sides as necessary. Studies show that a helmet does not keep a rider from spotting danger.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.2, 'Wear the Right Gear'

question: According to the manual, most motorcycle crashes happen:
choice_a: Only after several hours of continuous riding
choice_d: On short trips of less than five miles, just a few minutes after starting out
explanation: Most crashes happen on short trips (less than five miles long), just a few minutes after starting out.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.2, 'Wear the Right Gear'

question: At the speeds most crashes occur (under 30 mph), an approved helmet can cut the number and severity of head and neck injuries by about:
explanation: Most riders are riding slower than 30 mph when a crash occurs. At these speeds, helmets can cut both the number and severity of head and neck injuries by half.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.2, 'Wear the Right Gear'

question: No matter what speed a crash occurs at, helmeted riders are how much more likely than unhelmeted riders to survive a head injury?
explanation: No matter what the speed, helmeted riders are three times more likely to survive head injuries than those not wearing helmets at the time of the crash.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.2, 'Wear the Right Gear'

question: A label from which organization gives added assurance of helmet quality beyond meeting DOT and state standards?
explanation: A helmet should be designed to meet U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) and state standards; a label from the Snell Memorial Foundation also gives an assurance of quality.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.2, 'Helmet Selection'

question: The manual describes two primary types of helmets that provide different levels of coverage. What are they?
explanation: There are two primary types of helmets recommended, providing two different levels of coverage: three-quarter and full face.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.2, 'Helmet Selection'

question: For maximum protection, whichever helmet style a rider chooses, it should fit snugly all the way around and:
choice_a: Have no obvious defects such as cracks, loose padding, or frayed straps
choice_b: Be at least two sizes too large for airflow
choice_c: Only cover the top of the head
choice_d: Be worn without fastening the retention strap for comfort
explanation: Get the most protection from a helmet by making sure it fits snugly all the way around and has no obvious defects such as cracks, loose padding, or frayed straps.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.2, 'Helmet Selection'

question: A plastic impact-resistant faceshield helps protect a rider from all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_d: Pebbles thrown up from cars ahead
explanation: A plastic impact-resistant faceshield can help protect a rider's whole face in a crash, and also protects from wind, dust, dirt, rain, insects, and pebbles thrown up from cars ahead -- it has nothing to do with passenger balance.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Compared to a faceshield, goggles:
choice_b: Protect the whole face equally well
choice_c: Protect the eyes but not the rest of the face
choice_d: Are only effective in cold weather
explanation: Goggles protect a rider's eyes, though they won't protect the rest of the face like a faceshield does.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Can a windshield mounted on the motorcycle substitute for a faceshield or goggles?
choice_a: Only on motorcycles equipped with fairings
choice_b: Yes, a windshield alone is sufficient eye protection
choice_c: Yes, but only at speeds above 45 mph
choice_d: No -- most windshields will not protect the eyes from wind, and neither will eyeglasses or sunglasses
explanation: A windshield attached to the motorcycle is not a substitute for a faceshield or goggles. Most windshields will not protect the eyes from the wind, and neither will eyeglasses or sunglasses.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Do contact lenses qualify as protective eyewear for riding under Minnesota's equipment guidance?
choice_a: No -- riders are required to wear protective eyewear such as glasses, goggles, or a face shield even with a windscreen; contact lenses do not qualify
choice_b: Yes, contact lenses fully satisfy the eyewear requirement
choice_c: Yes, but only soft contact lenses
choice_d: Only if worn along with sunglasses
explanation: Motorcyclists are required to wear protective eyewear, such as glasses, goggles, or a face shield, even if the motorcycle has a windscreen. Contact lenses do not qualify as protective eyewear.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.IV, 'Protective Eyewear'

question: When should tinted eye protection not be worn?
choice_b: At night or any other time when little outside light is available
explanation: Tinted eye protection should not be worn when little outside light is available.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Wearing a protective jacket even in warm weather primarily helps:
explanation: Wear a jacket even in warm weather to prevent dehydration; many jackets are designed to protect without overheating the rider, even on summer days.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Clothing'

question: According to the manual, which material offers the most protection for a riding jacket and pants?
explanation: Jacket and pants should cover the arms and legs completely; leather offers the most protection, though sturdy synthetic material provides a lot of protection as well.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Clothing'

question: Riding boots or shoes should be:
choice_a: High and sturdy enough to cover and support the ankles, with hard, durable, slip-resistant soles
choice_c: Fitted with long, loose laces for quick removal
choice_d: Made with smooth leather soles for style
explanation: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover the ankles and give them support, with soles made of hard, durable, slip-resistant material; laces should be tucked in so they won't catch.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Clothing'

question: Riding gloves should be made of:
choice_b: Leather or a similarly durable material
choice_c: Any material, since gloves don't help in a crash
explanation: Gloves allow a better grip and help protect a rider's hands; they should be made of leather or similar durable material.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Clothing'

question: What does the manual say about hearing protection while riding?
choice_a: Hearing protection is illegal to wear while riding
choice_b: Hearing protection is unnecessary because a full-face helmet completely blocks all noise
choice_c: Long-term exposure to engine and wind noise can cause permanent hearing damage even with a full-face helmet, so hearing protection should be worn in line with state law
choice_d: Only passengers, never operators, need hearing protection
explanation: Hearing protection reduces noise while still allowing important sounds like horns or sirens to be heard. Long-term exposure to engine and wind noise can cause permanent hearing damage even if a rider wears a full-face helmet, so riders should follow state laws regarding hearing protection.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.3, 'Clothing'
